title: Community-acquired pneumonia (child)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, emergency department, paediatric ward
summary: Classify with WHO signs: fast breathing or chest indrawing without danger signs is pneumonia treated at home with oral amoxicillin (at least 40 mg/kg twice daily); any danger sign or hypoxaemia is severe pneumonia needing admission, oxygen and injectable ampicillin plus gentamicin.

sections.title: Assess and classify (WHO, age 2 to 59 months)
items: Fast breathing (count a full minute in a calm child): 50 breaths/min or more at 2 to 11 months, 40 or more at 12 to 59 months. Under 2 months, 60 or more: manage as possible serious bacterial infection.

Chest indrawing: the lower chest wall moves in on inspiration. Fast breathing and/or chest indrawing without danger signs is classed as pneumonia and treated with oral amoxicillin (WHO 2014, reconfirmed 2024).

General danger signs mean severe pneumonia: unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargy or unconsciousness, stridor in a calm child, or severe malnutrition. Hypoxaemia (SpO2 below 90%) also means severe disease.

No pulse oximeter: suspect hypoxaemia with head nodding, nasal flaring, grunting or severe tachypnoea (20 or more breaths/min above the age cut-off) (WHO 2024). WHO strongly advises pulse oximetry at every first-level facility.

BTS features of severe disease: SpO2 below 92% or cyanosis, respiratory rate above 70 (infants) or above 50 (older children), grunting, apnoea, not feeding or dehydration, capillary refill 2 seconds or more, or a chronic condition (heart, lung, immune).

Bacterial pneumonia is likely with persistent or repeated fever above 38.5 °C plus chest recession and a raised respiratory rate. Under 2 years, mild symptoms with wheeze and low-grade fever are usually viral and need no antibiotic (BTS).

sections.title: Investigations
items: Pneumonia managed at home: no routine chest X-ray, blood tests or microbiology (BTS, NICE).

Chest X-ray if admitted with severe disease, not improving, or a complication is suspected (dull percussion with absent breath sounds suggests effusion). Lung ultrasound is an alternative in trained hands (NICE 2025).
CRP and other acute phase reactants do not separate viral from bacterial pneumonia; do not measure them routinely.

Severe pneumonia: blood culture if sepsis is suspected, blood glucose, haemoglobin, and sodium, potassium and creatinine at baseline and daily while on IV fluids. Consider HIV testing where exposure is possible (it changes antibiotic choice).
Pleural fluid, if aspirated: microscopy, culture and pneumococcal antigen or PCR.

sections.title: Pneumonia without danger signs (outpatient)
items: Oral amoxicillin at least 40 mg/kg per dose twice daily (80 mg/kg/day) for 5 days (WHO). Fast breathing alone in low HIV prevalence areas: 3 days is enough.

Chest indrawing without danger signs: oral amoxicillin for 5 days as an outpatient rather than admission for injectables (WHO strong recommendation), with follow-up. Refer instead if HIV-infected or exposed, or if SpO2 is below 90%.

NICE 2025 uses lower age-banded doses and shorter courses: 3 days at 3 months to 11 years for uncomplicated non-severe pneumonia, 5 days under 3 months or at 12 years and over, extended if the child is not clinically stable.
Penicillin allergy, or suspected Mycoplasma in a school-age child: clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg twice daily (max 500 mg per dose) for the same duration (NICE).

Advise carers on fluids, fever control and danger signs. Return if not improving within 3 days, or at once with danger signs. Fever and breathing difficulty usually settle in 3 to 4 days; cough can last up to 4 weeks.

sections.title: Severe pneumonia (danger signs or hypoxaemia)
items: Give the first antibiotic dose and refer urgently. Admit; clear the airway, give oxygen, maintain fluids and feeds, and treat fever, hypoglycaemia and wheeze.

Oxygen if SpO2 is below 90% (WHO threshold); where oxygen is plentiful, BTS starts it at 92% or less and keeps SpO2 above 92%. Use nasal cannulae; escalate to high-flow or CPAP for rising work of breathing.
First line (WHO): ampicillin 50 mg/kg or benzylpenicillin 50 000 units/kg IV or IM every 6 hours, plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg IV or IM once daily, for at least 5 days.

Second line after failure: ceftriaxone 50 to 80 mg/kg IV or IM once daily (max 4 g/day). NICE first line is IV co-amoxiclav 30 mg/kg three times daily (max 1.2 g per dose), adding clarithromycin if an atypical pathogen is suspected.

HIV-infected or exposed infants with chest indrawing or severe pneumonia: ampicillin plus gentamicin, or ceftriaxone; add empirical co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis at 2 to 12 months (WHO), dosed per national HIV guidance.
Oral antibiotics work even in severe pneumonia if the child can take and keep them down (BTS). Review IV antibiotics by 48 hours and switch to oral amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav once improving.
Avoid nasogastric tubes in severely ill infants where possible (they compromise breathing). Chest physiotherapy does not help.

sections.title: Reassess and escalate
items: Reassess if fever persists 48 hours after starting treatment, work of breathing increases or the child becomes distressed or agitated: look for effusion or empyema, lung abscess, necrotising pneumonia, or another diagnosis (foreign body, TB, heart failure).
PICU referral: SpO2 not maintained above 92% on FiO2 above 0.6, shock, rising respiratory and heart rate with exhaustion (with or without rising CO2), or recurrent apnoea or slow irregular breathing.
Failure of first-line oral amoxicillin in the community: refer to a facility that can give second-line treatment.

sections.title: Special groups and India
items: Young infants under 2 months with fast breathing, chest indrawing or poor feeding: manage as possible serious bacterial infection (see Neonatal sepsis protocol).
Children aged 5 to 9 years: WHO makes no specific recommendation; use clinical assessment and amoxicillin as for younger children (BTS, NICE).
Severe acute malnutrition: treat as complicated SAM with parenteral antibiotics (see SAM protocol). Age under 12 months, malnutrition and HIV raise the risk of death.
India: IMNCI and the SAANS campaign follow the same WHO classification, with oral amoxicillin for pneumonia and referral with injectable antibiotics for severe pneumonia.

sections.title: Prevention and follow-up
items: Complete Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, measles and pertussis immunisation; give influenza vaccine where recommended.
Promote exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, good nutrition, hand washing, and reduce exposure to tobacco and cooking-fuel smoke.
Follow-up chest X-ray is not needed after uncomplicated recovery; consider it for round pneumonia, lobar collapse or persisting symptoms.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Counting the respiratory rate for less than a full minute, or in a crying child.
Giving antibiotics to infants with bronchiolitis or viral wheeze and no focal signs; reassess breathing rate and indrawing after treating the wheeze.
Not using a pulse oximeter; oximeters can overestimate SpO2 in darker skin.
Underdosing amoxicillin: pneumonia needs at least 40 mg/kg twice daily.
Missing TB, an inhaled foreign body, HIV or congenital heart disease when pneumonia recurs or fails to respond.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin (oral)
drugs.dose: At least 40 mg/kg per dose twice daily (80 mg/kg/day; max 2 g per dose) for 5 days
drugs.notes: WHO first line for fast breathing or chest indrawing pneumonia. 3 days for fast breathing alone in low HIV prevalence areas; NICE uses 3 days at 3 months to 11 years.

drugs.name: Ampicillin
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 6 hours (max 2 g per dose) for at least 5 days
drugs.notes: Severe pneumonia, with gentamicin. Alternative: benzylpenicillin 50 000 units/kg IV or IM every 6 hours.

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.dose: 7.5 mg/kg IV or IM once daily for at least 5 days
drugs.notes: With ampicillin or penicillin. Check renal function; measure levels where available.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 50 to 80 mg/kg IV or IM once daily (max 4 g/day)
drugs.notes: Second line after failure of ampicillin plus gentamicin; first-line option in HIV-infected or exposed children.

drugs.name: Co-amoxiclav (IV)
drugs.dose: 30 mg/kg IV three times daily (max 1.2 g per dose); twice daily at 1 to 2 months
drugs.notes: NICE first line for severe pneumonia; step down to oral co-amoxiclav to complete 5 days.

drugs.name: Clarithromycin
drugs.dose: 7.5 mg/kg orally or IV twice daily (max 500 mg per dose)
drugs.notes: Penicillin allergy or suspected atypical pathogen; NICE gives weight-banded oral doses.
